title: Storyteller in ADNI4: Application of an early Alzheimer’s disease screening tool using brief, remote, and speech-based testing

quick_read.tldr: This study tested Storyteller models developed in AMYPRED on ADNI4 clinic and remote cohorts. It found out-of-sample signal, but score thresholds shifted between cohorts, and diagnoses in the large remote cohort were primarily self-reported.
quick_read.problem_and_motivation: Speech-screening research often relies on small samples and internal cross-validation. The authors tested whether models generalize across study cohorts, devices, and populations.
quick_read.core_method: Speech features—including text similarity, lexical, temporal, and acoustic measures—were analyzed in AMYPRED (N=101), then tested in ADNI4’s in-clinic cohort (N=57) and remote digital cohort (N=426).
quick_read.key_results: The abstract reports AUCs of 0.71–0.84 for the best text-based models across cohorts. G-match AUCs were 0.82 in AMYPRED, 0.73 in ADNI4 in-clinic, and 0.75 in ADNI4 remote. Thresholds associated with similar sensitivity shifted across cohorts.
quick_read.why_it_matters: External validation is central to screening research, but a generalization signal does not make thresholds portable or establish clinical validity. The study used English-language materials and does not establish performance for Mandarin speakers or individual diagnosis.

detail.motivation: For large-scale prescreening, speech models need evaluation outside their development cohort and across different recruitment methods, devices, and demographic groups. The authors used ADNI4 clinic and remote cohorts to assess out-of-sample performance of the Storyteller task.

contributions.contribution: Developed/evaluated early-AD speech models in AMYPRED and tested them out of sample in ADNI4 clinic and remote cohorts.
Compared text-similarity, lexical, temporal, and acoustic features, and documented shifts in G-match score thresholds between cohorts.

research_questions.question: Do automatic story-recall models developed in AMYPRED generalize to ADNI4 clinic and remote cohorts with broader device and population variation?
research_questions.how: The authors extracted text-similarity, lexical, temporal, and acoustic features, developed/evaluated models in AMYPRED, and tested them on ADNI4 samples, comparing AUC and sensitivity-related thresholds.
research_questions.answer: G-match AUCs were 0.82 in AMYPRED, 0.73 in ADNI4 in-clinic, and 0.75 in ADNI4 remote. Discrimination persisted out of sample, but absolute score distributions and decision thresholds shifted.
research_questions.meaning: The findings support continued external validation; thresholds require reevaluation in each target population, while self-reported labels and the small clinic sample limit the strength of evidence.

detail.method: Three English-language story-recall samples were studied: AMYPRED (N=101, including 46 participants with MCI), ADNI4 in-clinic (N=57, including 13 with MCI), and ADNI4 remote digital (N=426, including 58 self-reporting MCI, mild AD, or dementia). The authors extracted text similarity (G-match), lexical, temporal, and acoustic features and evaluated predictions against clinical or self-reported labels. More than one-third of ADNI4 participants were from historically underrepresented populations.
detail.experiments_and_key_findings: The abstract reports AUCs of 0.71–0.84 across cohorts for the best text-similarity/lexical models. G-match AUCs for clinical or self-reported cognitive status were 0.82 in AMYPRED (95% CI 0.74–0.89), 0.73 in ADNI4 in-clinic (0.58–0.86), and 0.75 in remote digital (0.67–0.82). At approximately 0.70 sensitivity, the G-match threshold was about 66.9 in AMYPRED versus 57.7 and 57.8 in ADNI4 in-clinic and remote cohorts, respectively—evidence that score distributions and thresholds were not directly portable.

author_reported: The ADNI4 in-clinic sample with clinical diagnoses was small; the larger remote cohort relied on less robust self-reported diagnoses. Discussion §4.6.
Transcription error rates in ADNI4 were not yet fully evaluated; the authors called for research on transcription equity across demographic groups. Discussion §4.6.
Unsupervised remote recordings used different devices and microphones, potentially affecting audio quality. Discussion §4.6.
G-match absolute scores and thresholds for target sensitivity varied across cohorts. Discussion §4.1.
ai_analysis: All three cohorts used English-language materials; the study provides no direct evidence for Mandarin, dialects, bilingual speakers, or other educational/cultural contexts.

Remote self-reported diagnoses are less robust than clinical assessment, while the in-clinic cohort included only 57 participants; discrimination should not be read as definitive diagnostic performance.
Target-population prevalence changes PPV/NPV. Even with a similar AUC, deployment thresholds require prespecified calibration and independent validation.

Several authors disclosed employment or shareholding relationships with Novoic, the commercial developer of Storyteller; consider these disclosures alongside the out-of-sample results and validation design.

detail.relation_to_research: As a follow-up to earlier Aβ/cognitive-screening work, this paper asks whether speech-model signals persist outside their source cohort. For XiaoHang’s research direction, it highlights independent test cohorts, threshold stability, label quality, and cross-language fairness as central design questions—not just internal AUC.
detail.what_can_be_done_next: Conduct prospective, multicenter external validation in Chinese-speaking populations. Freeze feature extraction, model, and thresholds in advance; report AUC, sensitivity, specificity, calibration, and PPV/NPV by site, language/dialect, age, and education. Compare remote self-reports with standardized clinical assessments and biomarker-confirmed subsamples, and audit microphone variation, transcription errors, and dropout bias.

G-match AUCs in AMYPRED and both independent ADNI4 cohorts.
